question: Despite a population of under three million, this Caribbean island has produced a wildly disproportionate share of the fastest sprinters in Olympic history, including the world record holder over both 100m and 200m. Which country is it?

options.info: Home to Usain Bolt and a sprint pipeline built around a handful of elite high school athletics programs.
Also punches above its weight in sprinting, but hasn't matched Jamaica's Olympic sprint medal haul.
Strong in track relays, especially the 4x400m, but not the sprint powerhouse Jamaica is.
A cricket-mad Caribbean island, but not known for producing world-record sprinters.

question: At most major international marathons, from Boston to Berlin, the winner's podium is disproportionately filled with runners from a single East African country, often specifically from its Rift Valley highlands. Which country is it?

options.info: The high-altitude training grounds around Iten, in the Rift Valley, have produced generations of world-class distance runners.
A fierce distance-running rival with its own legendary marathoners, but trails Kenya in total major marathon wins.
Has produced standout distance runners like Joshua Cheptegei, but on a much smaller scale than Kenya.
Has a strong middle-distance tradition, but not the marathon dominance of Kenya.

question: In this West African nation, traditional wrestling matches — blending combat sport with pre-fight ritual dances, drumming, and amulets believed to bring luck — fill stadiums and turn top wrestlers into some of the country's highest-paid athletes. Which country is it?

options.info: The sport, called Laamb, is considered the national sport and predates French colonial rule by centuries.
Has its own traditional wrestling styles, but Laamb wrestling's commercial and cultural home is Senegal.
Shares some Sahelian wrestling traditions with Senegal, but the sport's center is Dakar, in Senegal.
A West African neighbor with a growing sports scene, but not the historic home of Laamb wrestling.

question: With more world championship medals than any gymnast in history, this American athlete has had multiple skills named after her across different apparatuses because they were considered too difficult for anyone to have landed before her. Who is she?

options.info: Her named skills include a triple-twisting double backflip on floor, nicknamed 'the Biles II.'
Scored gymnastics' first perfect 10 at the 1976 Olympics, a generation before Biles.
The first American gymnast to win Olympic all-around and team gold in the same games, but doesn't hold Biles's medal record.
The most decorated American gymnast before Biles, competing in the 1990s.

question: Between 1975 and 1979, one Caribbean cricket team assembled from several different island nations won the sport's first two World Cups and dominated Test cricket for nearly two decades behind a fearsome pace-bowling attack. What is this combined team called?

options.info: Represents multiple independent Caribbean nations, including Jamaica, Barbados, and Trinidad and Tobago, as a single international cricket team.
Was actually banned from international cricket for most of this era due to apartheid-related sporting boycotts.
A cricketing powerhouse with its own golden eras, but not the dominant force of the late 1970s.
Would win its own World Cup later, in 1996, a different era of the sport.

question: No national football team has lifted the FIFA World Cup trophy more times than this South American country, which has won it on five separate occasions between 1958 and 2002. Which country is it?

options.info: The only country to have played in every World Cup tournament ever held.
Has won the World Cup four times, one fewer than Brazil's record.
Has also won four World Cups, tied with Germany for second place on the all-time list.
Has won three World Cups, most recently in 2022.

question: Nicknamed 'the Master of Suspense,' this British director pioneered techniques like the shocking shower scene in 'Psycho' and made a cameo appearance in nearly every one of his own films. Who was he?

options.info: Directed over 50 films across six decades, including 'Vertigo,' 'Rear Window,' and 'North by Northwest.'
Directed and starred in 'Citizen Kane,' a contemporary working in a very different style.
An Austrian-born director known for films like 'Some Like It Hot' and 'Sunset Boulevard.'
A British director known for sweeping epics like 'Lawrence of Arabia,' rather than suspense thrillers.

question: Born in Taiwan, this director has moved fluidly between genres and languages, winning Best Director Oscars for both a wuxia martial arts epic and a survival tale about a boy adrift with a tiger. Who is he?

options.info: Won Oscars for 'Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon' and 'Life of Pi,' and also directed 'Brokeback Mountain.'
A Hong Kong director famous for stylized action films like 'Face/Off,' a different genre specialty.
A mainland Chinese director known for visually lush films like 'Hero' and 'Raise the Red Lantern.'
A Hong Kong director known for atmospheric, romantic dramas like 'In the Mood for Love.'

question: In 1975, a mechanical shark that kept malfunctioning during filming forced this young director to rely on suggestion and suspense rather than showing the creature directly — accidentally making 'Jaws' scarier and inventing the modern summer blockbuster. Who directed it?

options.info: Went on to direct 'E.T.,' 'Jurassic Park,' and 'Schindler's List' across a career spanning decades.
An American director known for zombie horror films like 'Night of the Living Dead,' a different genre entirely.
An American director known for horror and sci-fi films like 'Halloween' and 'The Thing.'
A British director known for 'Alien' and 'Blade Runner,' slightly later in the decade.

question: With 21 Academy Award nominations, this American actress holds the record for the most Oscar nominations of any performer in history, spanning roles from a Danish author in Africa to a fashion magazine editor. Who is she?

options.info: Has won three competitive Oscars, for 'Kramer vs. Kramer,' 'Sophie's Choice,' and 'The Iron Lady.'
Holds the record for the most competitive acting Oscar wins, with four, but far fewer nominations than Streep.
A celebrated British actress with multiple Oscar nominations, though well short of Streep's total.
An Australian actress with numerous nominations and two wins, but not as many nominations as Streep.

question: Released in 1995, this film was the first feature-length movie made entirely with computer animation, following a cowboy doll's rivalry with a new spaceman action figure. What is it called?

options.info: Produced by Pixar and directed by John Lasseter, it launched a franchise that would eventually span four films.
A landmark CGI film too, but released years later, in 2001, by a different studio.
An early computer-animated film from DreamWorks, released shortly after 'Toy Story' but not the first.
Pixar's second feature film, released in 1998, three years after 'Toy Story.'

question: Based on a still-unfinished series of fantasy novels, this HBO series about noble families fighting for control of a fictional continent became one of the most-watched and most-pirated shows in television history. What is it called?

options.info: Based on George R. R. Martin's 'A Song of Ice and Fire' novels, it ran for eight seasons starting in 2011.
Another acclaimed HBO drama, set in Baltimore and focused on crime and institutions, not fantasy.
An earlier HBO historical drama set in the ancient world, not a fantasy series.
A rival fantasy series based on Polish novels, but produced by Netflix, not HBO.

question: Listen to the clip below, then answer: which German composer wrote this fiery, tempo-shifting dance — one of a set of 21 he based on Roma folk melodies rather than composing entirely from scratch?

audio.credit: Fulda Symphonic Orchestra, cond. Simon Schindler, piano: Johannes Volker Schmidt — EFF Open Audio License, via Wikimedia Commons

options.info: Composed 21 Hungarian Dances based on Romani/Hungarian folk themes; No. 5 is by far the most famous.
Wrote his own "Slavonic Dances" in a similar folk-inspired style, but this isn't one of them.
Also drew heavily on Hungarian folk material in his "Hungarian Rhapsodies," but didn't compose this particular piece.
Norwegian composer known for incorporating folk melodies into concert works like "Peer Gynt," but not this piece.

question: Listen to the clip below — this piece is often performed today as a setting of the Latin prayer 'Ave Maria,' though the composer actually wrote it as a song about a different woman altogether, a character from a Walter Scott poem. Who composed it?

audio.credit: Performed by Dorothea Fayne (voice) and Uwe Streibel (piano) — CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

options.info: Composed "Ellens dritter Gesang" (Ellen's Third Song) for Walter Scott's poem "The Lady of the Lake"; its "Ave Maria" opening line led to its now-common association with the prayer.
Also wrote choral and vocal works, but not this piece.
Composed sacred vocal works of his own, but this isn't one of them.
A contemporary Romantic composer known for song cycles ("Lieder"), but didn't write this piece.

question: Watch the clip below — this 2003 chart-topper mixes hip hop and funk-pop, was performed almost entirely by one half of a duo (his bandmate barely appears on the track at all), and famously tells listeners to 'shake it like a Polaroid picture.' Which act recorded it?

audio.credit: OutKast – 'Hey Ya!' official video, via OutkastVEVO on YouTube

options.info: "Hey Ya!" was written and performed almost entirely by André 3000, with Big Boi largely absent from the track itself.
Another genre-blending 2000s duo (Cee-Lo Green and Danger Mouse), best known for "Crazy," released a few years later.
Also blended hip hop with pop hooks in the 2000s, but didn't record this particular song.
Pharrell Williams' rock-funk side project, active in the same era, but unrelated to this track.

question: Listen to this vintage-style cover below — big band horns and soulful vocals reworking a much harder-edged song. Which 1970s rock band recorded the original, a power ballad about chasing a dream until it comes true?

audio.credit: Cover: Postmodern Jukebox ft. Morgan James, via PostmodernJukebox on YouTube — original song by Aerosmith

options.info: "Dream On," from their 1973 debut album, is the original being covered here in a vintage soul style.
Another iconic 1970s rock act known for epic ballads, but didn't record this particular song.
Famous for arena rock ballads like "Don't Stop Believin'," from a slightly later era than this song.
Also known for emotionally driven rock songs in the 1970s, but not this one.

question: Besides painting what may be the most famous portrait in the world, this Renaissance polymath filled notebooks with mirror-written designs for flying machines, anatomical studies, and engineering concepts centuries ahead of his time. Who was he?

options.info: Painted both the 'Mona Lisa' and 'The Last Supper,' while also working as an engineer, inventor, and scientist.
A younger contemporary Renaissance painter, known for works like 'The School of Athens,' but not for the notebooks or inventions.
An earlier Renaissance sculptor, best known for his bronze statue of David.
A Renaissance architect and engineer famous for designing Florence Cathedral's dome, not the notebooks or paintings.

question: This contemporary Chinese artist and activist covered the floor of London's Tate Modern with a hundred million hand-painted porcelain sunflower seeds, and has used his art to criticize government censorship and human rights abuses, leading to his own detention in 2011. Who is he?

options.info: Helped design the 'Bird's Nest' stadium for the 2008 Beijing Olympics before later becoming an outspoken government critic.
Another contemporary Chinese artist, known for large-scale gunpowder and fireworks-based artworks.
A Chinese contemporary artist known for invented, illegible calligraphy-like scripts.
A Chinese painter known for haunting family-portrait style paintings from the 'Bloodline' series.

question: Known for room-sized mirrored installations filled with points of colored light and for covering surfaces in repetitive polka dots, this Japanese artist has voluntarily lived in a psychiatric institution since the 1970s, using art as a form of therapy. Who is she?

options.info: Her 'Infinity Mirror Rooms' have become some of the most photographed art installations in the world.
A Serbian performance artist known for endurance-based works, not polka dots or mirror rooms.
A Japanese-American conceptual artist and musician, married to John Lennon, working in a different medium.
An American photographer known for staged self-portraits in different characters and costumes.

question: Her X-ray diffraction image, known as 'Photo 51,' was crucial evidence for discovering the double-helix structure of DNA, but she died before the Nobel Prize was awarded for it in 1962 and initially received little public credit. Who was she?

options.info: Her image was shown to James Watson without her knowledge, and her contribution wasn't widely recognized until decades after her death.
An American geneticist who discovered 'jumping genes,' winning a Nobel Prize decades later, unrelated to DNA's structure.
A British chemist who won a Nobel Prize for determining the structures of important biomolecules using X-ray crystallography, but not DNA's structure.
An Italian neurobiologist who discovered nerve growth factor, unrelated to this DNA research.

question: This Serbian-American inventor championed alternating current for electrical power distribution, competing fiercely against Thomas Edison's rival direct current system in what's remembered as the 'War of the Currents.' Who was he?

options.info: His AC system, commercialized with backing from George Westinghouse, ultimately became the standard for power grids worldwide.
Championed direct current and ran a publicity campaign highlighting AC's dangers, but he was Tesla's rival, not the AC pioneer.
The businessman who financed and commercialized Tesla's AC patents, though the underlying invention was Tesla's.
An Italian inventor known for pioneering long-distance radio transmission, a different field entirely.

question: Her hand calculations of orbital mechanics were considered so reliable that astronaut John Glenn personally asked her to verify the electronic computer's numbers before his 1962 orbital flight. Who was this NASA mathematician?

options.info: Her story, along with fellow NASA mathematicians Dorothy Vaughan and Mary Jackson, was told in the film 'Hidden Figures.'
Led the software engineering team for NASA's Apollo Guidance Computer, a slightly later and different NASA contribution.
The first American woman in space, in 1983, decades after Johnson's calculations for Glenn's flight.
A Soviet cosmonaut and the first woman in space, in 1963, a different role from Johnson's ground-based calculations.

question: Often nicknamed 'the powerhouse of the cell' in biology classrooms, these bean-shaped organelles generate most of a cell's chemical energy and even carry their own small ring of DNA, separate from the cell's nucleus. What are they called?

options.info: Believed to have originated as free-living bacteria absorbed by ancient cells in a mutually beneficial partnership, a theory called endosymbiosis.
Cellular structures that build proteins by reading genetic instructions, but don't generate the cell's energy.
The energy-converting organelles found in plant cells specifically, using sunlight rather than the process mitochondria use.
Cellular structures that break down waste and cellular debris, sometimes nicknamed the cell's 'garbage disposal.'

question: In 1869, this Russian chemist arranged the known chemical elements by atomic weight and recurring properties into a table, leaving deliberate gaps for elements he predicted existed but hadn't yet been discovered. Who was he?

options.info: Several of his predicted 'missing' elements, including gallium and germanium, were discovered within his own lifetime, matching his forecasts closely.
An 18th-century French chemist often called the father of modern chemistry, who compiled an early list of elements decades before Mendeleev's table.
Discovered the elements polonium and radium later, but didn't create the periodic table itself.
An early 19th-century English chemist who developed modern atomic theory, before the periodic table existed.

question: Developed in 1935, this logarithmic scale for measuring earthquake magnitude means each whole-number increase represents roughly 32 times more released energy, not simply a linear step up. Whose name is it commonly associated with?

options.info: Developed the scale with colleague Beno Gutenberg at Caltech, though seismologists today mostly use updated moment magnitude scales instead.
An Italian volcanologist who developed an earlier scale measuring earthquake intensity based on observed damage, not a magnitude calculation.
Richter's close collaborator on the original scale, though it became publicly associated with Richter's name alone.
A British seismologist sometimes called the 'father of modern seismology' for his work on early seismographs, decades before this scale.

question: Built in the 15th century high in the Andes and abandoned within about a hundred years, this Inca citadel remained largely unknown to the outside world until an American historian was guided there by local farmers in 1911. What is it called?

options.info: Located in present-day Peru, it's now one of South America's most visited archaeological sites and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A famous Maya pyramid complex, but located in Mexico, not Peru.
An earlier pre-Inca archaeological site near Lake Titicaca in Bolivia, a different civilization and location.
A separate Inca fortress complex near Cusco, known for its massive interlocking stone walls.

question: Straddling the border of Nepal and Tibet, this is Earth's highest mountain above sea level, first confirmed summited in 1953 by a New Zealand beekeeper and a Nepali Sherpa mountaineer. What is it called?

options.info: Named after Sir George Everest, a former Surveyor General of India, though its Nepali name Sagarmatha and Tibetan name Chomolungma predate that.
The world's second-highest mountain, located in the Karakoram range on the Pakistan-China border.
The world's third-highest mountain, on the border of Nepal and India.
A notoriously dangerous Himalayan peak in Nepal, with one of the highest fatality rates among 8,000-meter mountains.

question: This Pacific island kingdom is the only country in Oceania never formally colonized by a foreign power, having instead negotiated a protectorate status with Britain that preserved its own monarchy. Which country is it?

options.info: Its monarchy traces back over a thousand years, making it one of the oldest continuous monarchies still in existence today.
Was administered first by Germany and later by New Zealand before gaining independence in 1962.
Was a British colony from 1874 until independence in 1970.
Was unusually jointly administered by both Britain and France as a condominium until 1980.

question: Built and rebuilt over centuries by successive Chinese dynasties to defend against nomadic invasions from the north, this fortification stretches for thousands of kilometers, though the popular claim that it's visible from space with the naked eye is a myth. What is it called?

options.info: Most of the sections tourists visit today, near Beijing, date from the later Ming dynasty.
Another massive Chinese infrastructure project, but a waterway connecting northern and southern China, not a wall.
A much smaller Roman fortification across northern Britain, built to mark the empire's frontier.
Stone enclosure walls built by the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe in southern Africa, an entirely separate structure.

question: Known for an advanced writing system, precise astronomical calendars, and step pyramids like those at Tikal and Chichen Itza, this civilization flourished across present-day Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, and Honduras for over a thousand years before Spanish contact. What is it called?

options.info: Rather than collapsing entirely, many Maya cities were already in decline before European contact, and Maya peoples and languages still exist today.
A later Mesoamerican civilization centered on the city of Tenochtitlan, in what's now central Mexico.
An earlier Mesoamerican civilization, sometimes called Mesoamerica's 'mother culture,' predating the Maya's peak by centuries.
A civilization centered in the Andes of South America, geographically and culturally distinct from Mesoamerica.

question: Aside from a brief occupation during World War II, this East African nation stands out for decisively defeating an invading European colonial army at the Battle of Adwa in 1896, preserving its independence at a time when most of the continent was being carved up by European powers. Which country is it?

options.info: Its victory over Italy at Adwa is still commemorated annually and made it a symbol of anti-colonial resistance across Africa.
Also avoided formal European colonization, but through a very different history, founded by freed African-American settlers with US backing.
Was ruled for decades as an Anglo-Egyptian condominium before gaining independence in 1956.
Was split between Italian and British colonial administrations before independence and later unification.

question: During the last Ice Age, falling sea levels exposed a land bridge across a narrow body of water separating two continents, allowing the first humans to walk from Asia into the Americas. What is this strait called today?

options.info: Named after Danish-Russian explorer Vitus Bering, who charted it for Russia in the 18th century.
Separates Europe from Africa at the western end of the Mediterranean, a different strait entirely.
The turbulent body of water between South America and Antarctica, notorious among sailors.
A major shipping route between the Malay Peninsula and the island of Sumatra, in Southeast Asia.

question: Carved directly into rose-colored sandstone cliffs by the Nabataean people over two thousand years ago, this ancient city in the desert of modern-day Jordan grew wealthy by controlling incense and spice trade routes, and later featured in a famous 'Indiana Jones' film. What is it called?

options.info: Its most famous structure, the Treasury, was carved as a tomb but is often mistaken for having been a bank or storehouse.
Another ancient desert trading city, but located in Syria rather than Jordan.
An ancient Roman temple complex in Lebanon, known for some of the largest stone blocks ever quarried.
An ancient Persian imperial capital in what's now Iraq, known for its massive brick archway.

question: Stretching roughly 6,400 kilometers and connecting Chinese silk producers to Mediterranean markets, this ancient network of trade routes also carried spices, ideas, religions, and, less deliberately, diseases like the bubonic plague between Asia and Europe. What is it commonly called?

options.info: The name itself was coined only in the 19th century by a German geographer, long after the trade routes' peak activity.
A separate, much shorter trade route carrying amber from the Baltic Sea south to the Mediterranean.
A trade network carrying frankincense and myrrh from Arabia toward the Mediterranean, a distinct but related network.
One of South Asia's oldest and longest roads, connecting the Indian subcontinent, but a different route.

question: From the 13th to 17th centuries, a confederation of merchant guilds and market towns along the Baltic and North Sea coasts banded together to protect shared trading interests, dominating commerce across Northern Europe for centuries without ever being a formal state. What was this confederation called?

options.info: Its most powerful member city, Lübeck, is still sometimes nicknamed the 'Queen of the Hanseatic League.'
A political union joining the crowns of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, a different kind of Nordic alliance.
A sprawling, loosely organized political entity covering much of Central Europe, but not a merchant trade confederation.
A German crusading military order that controlled territory along the Baltic coast, related but distinct from the merchant league.

question: Fought intermittently between 1337 and 1453 over succession to the French throne, this conflict between two royal houses actually lasted 116 years and featured figures like Joan of Arc before the French side ultimately prevailed. What is it called?

options.info: Despite the name, it wasn't one continuous war but a series of related conflicts across more than a century.
A later English civil war between two rival branches of the House of Plantagenet, fought after this conflict ended.

options.text: The War of the Spanish Succession
options.info: A later, separate European conflict fought in the early 18th century over the Spanish throne.
A separate, later and even more devastating conflict, fought largely across Central Europe in the 17th century.

question: During the brutal winter of 1939-40, this small Nordic country fought off a much larger Soviet invasion for over three months, inflicting disproportionate casualties partly through ski-mobile troops fighting in extreme cold, before eventually ceding some territory in peace talks. Which country was it?

options.info: The conflict is remembered as the Winter War, and Finnish resistance became a symbol of small-nation resilience.
Was invaded by Nazi Germany the following year, in 1940, a separate conflict from the Winter War.
A Baltic state annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940 without the sustained armed resistance Finland mounted.
Was invaded by both Germany and the Soviet Union in 1939, but in a different campaign from the Winter War.

question: When Soviet forces blockaded all road and rail access to a divided city in 1948, Western allies responded by flying in food, fuel, and supplies around the clock for nearly a year, keeping the city's residents fed without breaking the blockade militarily. What is this operation called?

options.info: At its peak, cargo planes were landing in West Berlin roughly every 90 seconds.
A broader American program of economic aid to rebuild Western Europe after World War II, not this specific airlift.
The Allied invasion of Normandy in 1944, an earlier and unrelated World War II operation.
A later 1968 period of political liberalization in Czechoslovakia, crushed by a Soviet-led invasion — unrelated to Berlin.

question: Created in 1999 by a Japanese designer working for a mobile phone company, these small digital pictographs were originally just 176 simple 12-by-12 pixel images meant to make phone messages more expressive. What are they called?

options.info: The word comes from Japanese 'e' (picture) and 'moji' (character) — its resemblance to the English word 'emotion' is just a coincidence.
The earlier, older concept of building faces from punctuation marks like ':-)', a text-based predecessor to emoji.
Japanese-style emoticons built from a wider range of characters, like '(^_^)', distinct from true pictographic emoji.
Larger, more detailed illustrated images used in messaging apps, a separate and later feature from emoji.

question: After a French newspaper mistakenly published his obituary while he was still alive, condemning him as a 'merchant of death' for inventing dynamite, this Swedish industrialist rewrote his will to fund a set of prizes meant to reward benefits to humanity instead. Who was he?

options.info: His prizes, first awarded in 1901, now span physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, peace, and later economics.
A Scottish-American steel magnate known for large-scale philanthropy, particularly funding public libraries, not the Nobel Prizes.
An American oil magnate whose foundation funded major philanthropic work, unrelated to the Nobel Prizes.
A British businessman whose fortune founded the Rhodes Scholarship, a different prestigious award.

question: Despite its Japanese name, this number-placement puzzle was actually invented in the United States in the late 1970s under the name 'Number Place,' and only became a worldwide craze after a Japanese puzzle company popularized and renamed it. What is it called?

options.info: The Japanese name roughly translates to 'single number,' referring to the rule that each digit can appear only once per row, column, and box.
Another Japanese-popularized number puzzle, involving crossword-style grids and sums, distinct from sudoku.
A picture logic puzzle solved by filling in grid squares according to numeric clues, unrelated to sudoku's number-placement rules.
A newer arithmetic-based grid puzzle invented by a Japanese math teacher, similar in spirit but not the same puzzle as sudoku.

question: In 1957, two engineers trying to invent a textured wallpaper accidentally sealed air bubbles between two shower curtains instead, and after that idea flopped, they successfully repurposed it as protective packaging material. What is it called?

options.info: Was also briefly marketed as greenhouse insulation before its packaging use took off, and is now a trademarked Sealed Air Corporation brand name.
A separate rigid foam packaging and insulation material, made from polystyrene, invented earlier by Dow Chemical.
Loose foam packing material used to fill empty space in boxes, a different invention from bubble wrap.
A plastic film that tightens around a product when heated, a distinct packaging technology.

question: Harvested by hand from the tiny crimson threads at the center of a specific crocus flower, with each flower producing only three usable strands, this is by weight the most expensive spice in the world. What is it called?

options.info: It can take well over 150 flowers, all picked by hand, to yield just a single gram of the dried spice.
The second most expensive spice by weight, derived from the seed pods of an orchid, and also labor-intensive to produce.
Sometimes called the 'queen of spices,' valuable but far less expensive than saffron by weight.
A tangy, deep-red spice used widely in Middle Eastern cooking, but far more affordable than saffron.

question: Its name literally stands for 'Water Displacement, 40th attempt' — the successful formula a small California company landed on after 39 earlier tries while trying to develop a rust-preventing solvent for the aerospace industry. What product is it?

options.info: Originally developed in 1953 to protect the outer skin of Atlas missiles from corrosion, long before it became a household name.
A petroleum jelly product with an unrelated origin story, discovered by a chemist noticing oil-rig workers using rod wax to heal cuts.
An older lubricating oil brand, but not the product behind this particular naming story.
A brand of adhesives and sealants, with a different corporate origin from WD-40.

question: Written in 1899 as the closing number of a patriotic pageant staged to raise money for journalists silenced by Russian censorship, this tone poem became so politically charged that it was sometimes programmed under bland decoy titles to get past the authorities. Its calm hymn-like section was later given words and is now sung almost as an unofficial national anthem. Which composer wrote it?

options.info: 'Finlandia' made him a national figure at 34; he then wrote almost nothing at all in the last thirty years of his life.
The leading Danish symphonist of the same generation, with a very different, more combative harmonic language.
The Norwegian whose miniatures and 'Peer Gynt' music had already given Nordic music an international audience.
A Swedish composer and conductor of the era, admired at home but far less known abroad.

question: Left almost totally blind at the age of three by a diphtheria epidemic, he composed in Braille and then dictated note by note to a copyist. In 1939 he wrote a concerto named after the gardens of a royal palace south of Madrid, whose slow movement — a plaintive cor anglais melody answered by the soloist — turned the classical guitar into a concerto instrument. Who was he?

options.info: He said the 'Concierto de Aranjuez' was about the scent of magnolias and birdsong; his wife later wrote that the slow movement mourned their lost first child.
The guitarist who spent his career persuading composers to write for the instrument — but he did not write this piece and initially disliked it.
The older Spanish composer of 'The Three-Cornered Hat', who wrote only one short work for solo guitar.
His piano suite 'Iberia' is so guitar-like that guitarists have adopted much of it, but he died in 1909.

question: In June 1933 the Chicago Symphony Orchestra performed her Symphony in E minor at the Century of Progress world's fair — the first time a major American orchestra had played a symphony by a Black woman. She then slipped out of the repertoire almost entirely, until in 2009 a couple renovating a derelict house in St. Anne, Illinois, found boxes of her manuscripts inside. Who was she?

options.info: Trained in Boston, she had fled Arkansas after a lynching. Her rediscovered scores are now recorded and programmed worldwide.
A Chicago pianist and composer who studied with the correct answer here and premiered her piano concerto.
The first Black American to earn a master's degree in music, better known as a critic than a composer.
A prolific composer of choral music, sometimes called the dean of Black women composers, active a generation later.

question: A short yelp recorded in 1951 for a western — a soldier being dragged under by an alligator — sat forgotten in a studio sound library until film-school graduates dug it out in the 1970s and began smuggling it into their own films as a private joke. It has since turned up in hundreds of movies, from space battles to Disney cartoons, and is named after a minor character in a 1953 western who used it. What is it?

options.info: Sound designer Ben Burtt identified the reel and named it; he then put it in Star Wars and Indiana Jones, and the tradition spread.
A real rival stock scream, sometimes called the 'Howie long scream', used in far fewer films.
A genuine stock effect — a thunderclap recorded in 1931 and reused for decades in horror films and cartoons.
Also a real reused effect: the yodelling falling cry from Disney shorts, recycled since the 1940s.

question: In 1951 a Baltimore hospital took a tissue sample from a 31-year-old tobacco farmer and mother of five being treated for cervical cancer. Unlike every previous sample, her cells kept dividing indefinitely in culture — the first immortal human cell line. They were used to test the polio vaccine, flown into orbit, and sold around the world for decades, all without her family's knowledge or consent. Whose cells were they?

options.info: The HeLa line has featured in tens of thousands of studies. Her family reached an agreement with the US National Institutes of Health over access to the genome only in 2013.
The New York cook known as 'Typhoid Mary', an asymptomatic carrier detained for decades — a very different kind of medical-consent case.
The first Black American woman to earn a chemistry doctorate, whose research linked cholesterol to clogged arteries.
The chemist who developed the first effective injectable treatment for leprosy, and died at 24 before publishing it.

question: In 1945 an engineer at the defence firm Raytheon was standing next to a running magnetron — a component built for radar sets — when he noticed the snack in his pocket had turned to goo. He sent out for popcorn kernels, which duly popped, and tried an egg next, which exploded over a colleague. Which everyday appliance grew out of that accident?

options.info: Percy Spencer's first commercial model, the 1947 Radarange, stood nearly two metres tall and was water-cooled.
Also electromagnetic, but it heats the pan itself by inducing currents in metal, and reached kitchens much later.
Predates this by decades — the pop-up mechanism was patented in 1919.
A 17th-century invention of Denis Papin's, refined for home use long before radar existed.
